messages.subject: Fwd: Re: [seewave] acoustat function
parts:
Re-bonjour,

Thanks for the rapid answer.
 I'm glad you agree about frequency limits.

You write that there is no squaring step but powers are squares (the square of the length of an amplitude vector -  obtained by multiplying a complex DFT result by its complex conjugate - Pythagoras

). That's what I meant by "squaring".

Krzysz
-------- Original Message --------
Subject: Re: [seewave] acoustat function
Date: 30-01-2014 10:51
From: Jerome Sueur <su...@mnhn.fr>
To: see...@googlegroups.com
Reply-To: 

 
Bonjour Krzysz,

 Thank you very much for your very useful comments.
 I will certainly add an argument for frequency limits in the next
version of seewave, coming not soon... I am afraid...
 Please note that there is no squaring step, neither for the spectral
nor for the time contours.
 All the best,
 Jerome 

 Le 30/01/2014 09:16, krzysztof...@inserm.fr a écrit :

> Bonjour Jerôme,
> Meilleurs voeux pour la nouvelle année.
> 
> I have been looking at the new acoustat routine in v1.7.3 (along with
> the papers on it). A couple of observations, please correct me if I'm
> wrong:
> 
> As far as I can see, calculating the "aggregate power spectrum" via
> the DFT _only_ has an advantage if one uses it for low (and/or high)
> frequency noise elimination. This could be done easily, with an added
> user-selected parameter in the command line and only a minor addition
> to the coding (in the f.cont lines?).
> To do it, instead of summing the power at every frequency band in a
> DFT, one only sums the powers above a minumum frequency and then noise
> below that frequency is eliminated from the spectrum. Of course it
> only works for sounds that are not "buried" in the noise
> (vocalisations in the 0-2kHz range for example) but then the user
> could set the minimum frequency to 0. High frequency noise could also
> be eliminated this way but I've never met it as a problem. (Fristrup &
> Watkins remove noise before the calculation but maybe whale
> vocalisations are buried in aquatic noise, Cortopassi also insists on
> prior noise-removal but most song bird vocalisations are above 2kHz
> and the above method seems simpler and less error-prone).
> 
> Otherwise, without this noise reduction, using DFTs for the
> calculation seems excessive. With DFT windows of _n_ samples, the
> "aggregate power spectrum" merely corresponds to the squared sum, over
> _n_ samples, of the sound amplitudes in each (overlapping) window of
> the time domain spectrum, i.e. a smoothed and squared time domain
> spectrum. This can be calculated much more simply and rapidly without
> calculating the DFTs and without the corresponding (small) errors
> introduced.
> 
> For those tempted to try it, the aggregate power spectrum, with noise
> elimination, should be useful for automatic detection of sound element
> lengths and intervals BUT the squaring causes a problem because it
> magnifies amplitude fluctuations within an element. Using a log (dB)
> scale may overcome this.
> 
> All the best,
> Krzysz
